c.tagline: Morocco's 'Blue Pearl,' a Rif Mountain medina where every wall is washed in shades of blue
langs: Spanish (common given historic ties to Spain)

card: Accepted at larger hotels and riads; cash preferred in the medina's shops and cafes

taxi.fareNote: Petit taxis are the local standard; agree the fare before departure if the meter isn't used

emergency.note: Tourist police can assist in major destinations; response times vary in smaller towns

walk: The medina is compact, hilly, and entirely walkable (car-free in the historic core); Akchour waterfalls require a car or organized tour

safety.safety: Very safe town, popular with independent travelers and photographers
safety.crime: Persistent unofficial guides and occasional hashish offers (illegal) in the surrounding hills are the main hassle, not violent crime

hood_landmark.Uta el-Hammam Square: Plaza Uta el Hammam and the Kasbah fortress
hood_landmark.Spanish Mosque Hill: The Spanish Mosque's hilltop sunset viewpoint
hood_landmark.Ras el-Ma: Ras el-Ma spring and waterfall at the medina's edge
hood_landmark.Talassemtane National Park (day-trip): The Akchour waterfalls and God's Bridge rock arch

avoid.reason: Relaxed, but hashish touts are persistent; otherwise safe

hood_desc: The famous blue-painted old town, a maze of photogenic alleys, dye shops, and guesthouses; the essential base for any visit.
The medina's lively central square, ringed by the Kasbah fortress, cafes, and the Grand Mosque.
A short uphill walk from the medina to a ruined mosque with the best panoramic sunset view over the blue town.
A natural spring and waterfall at the edge of the medina, traditionally used for washing wool, now a scenic stop.
A national park about 45 minutes away with waterfalls and hiking trails through the Rif Mountains.

water.note: Mountain-fed tap water is drunk by locals, but visitors usually stick to bottled to be safe.

transit.sys: Petit taxis around town; the medina itself is car-free
transit.map: Not centrally published; the medina is compact enough to navigate on foot
transit.note: Most visitors arrive by grand taxi or bus from Tangier, Tetouan, or Fes and explore the town entirely on foot

transport.air: Tangier Ibn Battouta Airport (TNG), about 2 hr away, is the nearest major airport
transport.train: No direct rail to Chefchaouen; nearest station is Tetouan, connected by bus/taxi
transport.bus: CTM and local buses connect to Tangier, Tetouan, and Fes
transport.car: Well connected via mountain roads from Tangier and Tetouan; grand taxis are a common shared-transport option

airport.name: Tangier Ibn Battouta Airport
airport.transport: Grand taxi, bus, or private transfer

net.w: Free wifi standard in riads and cafes
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in riads
net.ap: A Maroc Telecom or Orange Morocco tourist SIM or eSIM

food.name: Bissara
food.desc: Thick puree of dried split fava beans finished with olive oil, cumin and paprika, eaten with bread for breakfast on cold Rif mornings.

places.name: Beldi Bab Ssour
places.note: Home-style northern cooking; the bissara and goat tagines are the house specialities.

places.name: Sofia Restaurant
places.note: Its bissara is widely called the best in town, rich and creamy under a pool of olive oil.

places.name: Chez Hicham
places.note: Patio and rooftop terrace on the main square, good bissara and vegetarian tagines.

food.name: Jben (fresh goat cheese)
food.desc: Soft, mild white goat cheese made in the Rif villages around the town, served with bread, olives, olive oil and sometimes honey.

places.name: Souk stalls, Plaza Uta el-Hammam
places.note: Village women sell fresh jben wrapped in palm leaves on market mornings; buy early.

places.name: Beldi Bab Ssour
places.note: Serves local jben as a starter with khobz and olives alongside the Rif menu.

places.name: Casa Hassan / Restaurant Tissemlal
places.note: One of the oldest riad restaurants in the medina, cooking with local cheese and produce.

food.name: Tagine
food.desc: Slow-cooked in a conical clay pot - goat with onions, chicken with preserved lemon and olives, or kefta baked with egg and tomato.

places.name: Beldi Bab Ssour
places.note: Goat tagine is what the kitchen is known for; small room, so arrive early or try its sister.

places.name: Lala Mesouda
places.note: Second outpost of Beldi Bab Ssour with the identical menu and usually easier to get a table.

places.name: Casa Aladdin
places.note: Multi-level restaurant with a rooftop overlooking the square and the Rif mountains.

food.name: Msemen and harcha
food.desc: Flaky square msemen pancakes and gritty semolina harcha, griddled to order and eaten with honey, amlou almond paste or fresh cheese.

places.name: Bab el-Ain bakeries
places.note: Griddle stalls just inside the main gate cook msemen from dawn for a few dirhams.

places.name: Cafe Clock Chefchaouen
places.note: Breakfast plates of Moroccan breads with amlou and preserves in a restored medina house.

places.name: Plaza Uta el-Hammam cafes
places.note: Square-side cafes serve breakfast breads with mint tea from early morning.

food.name: Couscous
food.desc: Hand-rolled semolina steamed over a broth of seven vegetables with lamb or chicken, traditionally the Friday lunch after prayers.

places.name: Casa Aladdin
places.note: Reliable Friday couscous with a rooftop view over the blue medina.

places.name: Lala Mesouda
places.note: Home-cooked northern menu with couscous served the traditional way in a wide dish.

places.name: Casa Hassan / Restaurant Tissemlal
places.note: Set traditional menus in a historic riad, couscous among the mainstays.

food.name: Kefta brochettes
food.desc: Spiced minced lamb or beef pressed onto skewers and grilled over charcoal, served with khobz, cumin salt and a tomato-onion salad.

places.name: Chez Hicham
places.note: Square-side grill and terrace; brochettes and kefta tagine are the go-to orders.

places.name: Avenue Hassan I grills
places.note: Row of charcoal grill counters where locals eat brochettes at half medina prices.

places.name: Beldi Bab Ssour
places.note: Grills lamb and offal skewers alongside the tagines; small, honest kitchen.

food.name: Mint tea
food.desc: Green gunpowder tea steeped with a fistful of fresh Rif spearmint and plenty of sugar, poured from height into small glasses.

places.name: Plaza Uta el-Hammam cafes
places.note: The classic spot to sit for an hour with a pot of tea and watch the square.

places.name: Cafe Clock Chefchaouen
places.note: Rooftop terrace with mountain views; tea plus cultural events in the evenings.

places.name: Casa Aladdin
places.note: Upper terraces are the best sunset perch over the blue town for a glass of tea.

food.name: Fresh orange and avocado juice
food.desc: Hand-pressed orange juice from the carts, or the thick Moroccan avocado shake blended with milk, almonds and a little sugar.

places.name: Bab el-Ain juice stalls
places.note: Juice carts at the main gate press oranges to order all day for a couple of dirhams.

places.name: Plaza Uta el-Hammam cafes
places.note: Most square cafes blend avocado and banana shakes as well as fresh citrus.

places.name: Chez Hicham
places.note: Reliable fresh juices on the terrace, a good stop between medina walks.

landmarks: The Blue Medina (old town)
A maze of powder-blue lanes tumbling down the Rif foothills, this dreamlike walled quarter is Morocco's most photogenic townscape and the reason travelers make the pilgrimage here.
Kasbah of Chefchaouen (Kasbah Museum)
A restored 15th-century earthen fortress with a leafy Andalusian garden, ethnographic museum, and a tower whose ramparts frame the blue city against the mountains.
Plaza Uta el-Hammam
The medina's buzzing main square, ringed by cafes, mosaic fountains, and mulberry trees, where locals and travelers linger over mint tea beneath the kasbah walls.
Grand Mosque (Jamaa Bouzafar)
Chefchaouen's 15th-century principal mosque is famed for its rare octagonal red-toned minaret, an elegant landmark rising above the blue rooftops of the old town.
Spanish Mosque viewpoint (Jemaa Bouzafar hilltop)
An abandoned 1920s hilltop mosque reached by a short scenic walk, delivering the classic sunset panorama over the entire blue-washed city and surrounding Rif peaks.
Ras El Maa waterfall and springs
Just outside Bab El Ansar gate, this gushing mountain spring is where locals wash carpets and gather, offering a cool, sociable slice of everyday Chefchaouen life.
Akchour Waterfalls
A spectacular day-trip hike through the Talassemtane gorge to turquoise pools and cascades, the Rif Mountains' most rewarding natural excursion from the blue city.
God's Bridge (Pont de Dieu)
A colossal natural rock arch spanning the Farda River near Akchour, its 25-meter red-stone vault is among northern Morocco's most dramatic geological sights.
Talassemtane National Park
A UNESCO-recognized biosphere of cedar and fir forests wrapping the mountains above town, laced with hiking trails, Berber villages, and sweeping Rif viewpoints.
Bab el-Ain gate and Callejon El Asri
The medina's picturesque main gateway leads to its most photographed blue stairway alley, a flower-potted passage that has become an icon of Chefchaouen itself.

train.note: Chefchaouen has no railway. The nearest ONCF stations (https://www.oncf-voyages.ma/) are at Tangier, about 2h30 north by road, and Fes, roughly 4 hours south - both are on the national network with high-speed links to Casablanca. Everyone arrives by coach or grand taxi.

bus.note: No international coaches start here. CTM (https://www.ctm.ma/) is the reliable operator, running from the bus station below the medina to Tangier in about 2h30, Fes in 4 and Tetouan in 90 minutes - book online, as the daily services sell out in high season. The station is a steep 20-minute walk or a cheap petit taxi from the blue old town. Shared grand taxis to Tetouan leave when full.

ferry.note: Chefchaouen sits in the Rif mountains with no navigable water, so there are no ferries. The nearest crossings to Spain are at Tangier and Tanger Med, about 2h30 away, and Ceuta, which is a Spanish enclave reachable by road.

half.name: Tetouan
half.blurb: A UNESCO-listed medina blending Andalusian and Moroccan architecture, once the diplomatic capital of Spanish Morocco.

half.name: Ouazzane
half.blurb: A quieter hill town and Sufi religious center with a whitewashed medina and views over the surrounding olive groves.

full.name: Tangier
full.blurb: A historic port city on the Strait of Gibraltar with a labyrinthine kasbah, seafront corniche and literary café culture.

full.name: Asilah
full.blurb: A whitewashed Atlantic coastal town known for its mural-covered ramparts, art festival and Portuguese-built sea walls.

full.name: Ceuta
full.blurb: A Spanish enclave on the North African coast, reached via the border at Fnideq, with a fortified old town.
